\begin{infobox}{Conventions (identical to the Question Paper)}
\footnotesize
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item $a \bmod N$ is the remainder in $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$; the \textbf{order} $r = \operatorname{ord}_N(a)$ is the least $r > 0$ with $a^r \equiv 1 \pmod N$ (defined for $\gcd(a, N) = 1$);
      $\varphi$ is Euler's totient, $\lambda$ the Carmichael function. ``Factors'' means non-trivial factors ($1 < p < N$).
\item \textbf{Reduction:} if $r$ is even and $a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 \pmod N$, then $\gcd(a^{r/2} - 1, N)$ and $\gcd(a^{r/2} + 1, N)$ are non-trivial factors; otherwise the attempt fails.
\item \textbf{Circuit:} $t$ counting qubits (Hadamards), work register in $\ket1$, controlled $U_{a^{2^j} \bmod N}$ with $U_c\ket y = \ket{cy \bmod N}$ for $y < N$, inverse QFT, measurement of the
      counting register giving $y \in \{0, \dots, 2^t - 1\}$ (most significant bit first). \textbf{Post-processing:} \texttt{Fraction(y, 2**t).limit\_denominator(N)} gives $s/r'$;
      the order is $r'$ or its smallest multiple $kr'$ with $a^{kr'} \equiv 1$. $y = 0$ gives no candidate.
\item \textbf{Notebook} (\texttt{Shor.ipynb}, defaults): $N = 15$, $a = 7$, $n = $ \texttt{N.bit\_length()} work qubits, $t = 2n$ counting qubits, multipliers as exact
      permutation matrices (\texttt{cudaq.register\_operation}), $1000$ shots. \textbf{Previously recorded run}: CUDA-Q 0.16.0, CPU target \texttt{qpp-cpu}, no GPU; $12$ qubits,
      $51$ gates (plus $8$ measurements), outcomes $0, 64, 128, 192$; $0.766$ of the shots gave $15 = 3 \times 5$. No physical quantum processor was used.
\item State-vector memory: $16$ bytes per amplitude ($2^q$ amplitudes for $q$ qubits). $1$ MB $= 10^6$ bytes, $1$ GB $= 10^9$ bytes.
\end{itemize}
\end{infobox}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{1}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Euclidean algorithm}
Using the Euclidean algorithm, $\gcd(1071, 462)$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$21$ & \optlabel{B}\,$7$ & \optlabel{C}\,$147$ & \optlabel{D}\,$42$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $21$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The Euclidean algorithm replaces $(a, b)$ by $(b, a \bmod b)$ until the remainder is $0$; the last non-zero remainder is the $\gcd$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)$: $1071 = 2\cdot462 + 147$, $462 = 3\cdot147 + 21$, $147 = 7\cdot21 + 0$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $1071 = 2\cdot462 + 147$; $\ 462 = 3\cdot147 + 21$; $\ 147 = 7\cdot21 + 0$. The last non-zero remainder is $21$.
\emph{Check}: $1071 = 3^2\cdot7\cdot17$ and $462 = 2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11$, common part $3\cdot7 = 21$. The algorithm needs $O(\log N)$ division steps,
which is why the gcd steps of Shor's algorithm are classically cheap.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $7$ divides both numbers, but so does $21 = 3\cdot7$; $7$ is a common divisor, not the greatest one.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $147$ is the first remainder of the algorithm, not its last non-zero remainder; $147 \nmid 462$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $42$ does not divide $1071$ (odd), so it cannot be a common divisor at all.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The final $\gcd$ step of Shor's algorithm is this fast classical algorithm: $O(\log N)$ division steps.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{2}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Modular inverse}
The multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $20$ (the $b$ with $3b \equiv 1 \pmod{20}$, $0 < b < 20$) is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$7$ & \optlabel{B}\,$13$ & \optlabel{C}\,$17$ & \optlabel{D}\,$3$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $7$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} An inverse modulo $m$ exists iff $\gcd(b, m) = 1$; it is found by the extended Euclidean algorithm or by testing.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $3b \equiv 1 \pmod{20}$: $3\cdot7 = 21 = 20 + 1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Extended Euclid: $20 = 6\cdot3 + 2$, $3 = 1\cdot2 + 1$, so $1 = 3 - 2 = 3 - (20 - 6\cdot3) = 7\cdot3 - 20$. Hence $3\cdot7 = 21 \equiv 1 \pmod{20}$,
$b = 7$. The inverse exists because $\gcd(3, 20) = 1$; the same condition $\gcd(a, N) = 1$ makes multiplication by $a$ modulo $N$ reversible.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $3\cdot13 = 39 \equiv 19 \equiv -1 \pmod{20}$: $13$ is the inverse of $-3$, not of $3$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $3\cdot17 = 51 \equiv 11 \pmod{20}$, which is not $1$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $3$ is the number itself; $3\cdot3 = 9 \not\equiv 1 \pmod{20}$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Invertibility of $a$ modulo $N$ is exactly what makes the multiplier $U_a$ a permutation (unitary).
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{3}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Euler's totient $\varphi(pq)$}
Euler's totient $\varphi(91)$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$84$ & \optlabel{B}\,$90$ & \optlabel{C}\,$78$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$72$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $72$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Euler's totient counts the residues coprime to $N$; it is multiplicative for coprime factors.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\varphi(pq) = (p - 1)(q - 1)$ for distinct primes: $\varphi(7\cdot13) = 6\cdot12 = 72$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $91 = 7\cdot13$ with distinct primes, so $\varphi(91) = (7-1)(13-1) = 6\cdot12 = 72$: the number of $1 \le a \le 91$ coprime to $91$.
$90 = N - 1$ would hold only for a prime $N$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $84 = 91 - 7$ removes only the multiples of $13$ ($7$ of them) and forgets the multiples of $7$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $90 = 91 - 1$ would be $\varphi$ of a prime; $91 = 7\cdot13$ is composite.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $78 = 91 - 13$ removes only the multiples of $7$ and forgets the multiples of $13$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Knowing $\varphi(N)$ is equivalent to knowing the factors of an RSA modulus.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{4}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Multiplicative order}
The multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $11$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$11$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$10$ & \optlabel{C}\,$2$ & \optlabel{D}\,$5$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $10$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The order is the least $r > 0$ with $a^r \equiv 1$; it divides $\varphi(N)$ (Lagrange).

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Powers of $2$ mod $11$: $2, 4, 8, 5, 10, 9, 7, 3, 6, 1$ --- the first $1$ is at $r = 10$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Powers of 2 mod 11: $2, 4, 8, 5, 10, 9, 7, 3, 6, 1$ --- the first 1 appears at exponent $10$. The order divides $\varphi(11) = 10$, so the only
candidates are $1, 2, 5, 10$: $2^2 = 4$, $2^5 = 32 \equiv 10 \equiv -1$, so the order is $10$ ($2$ is a primitive root mod 11).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $11$ is the modulus; orders modulo a prime $p$ divide $p - 1 = 10$, so $11$ is impossible.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $2^2 = 4 \ne 1$; $2$ is the base, not its order.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $2^5 = 32 \equiv 10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$, not $1$; $5$ divides $10$ but is not the order.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Order finding is the hard problem; for tiny $N$ we can list powers, for RSA sizes we cannot.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{5}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Repeated squaring}
Using repeated squaring, $3^{13} \bmod 17$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$5$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$12$ & \optlabel{C}\,$3$ & \optlabel{D}\,$16$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $12$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Repeated squaring computes $a^{2^k}$ by squaring and multiplies the powers selected by the binary digits of the exponent.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $13 = 8 + 4 + 1$; $3^2 = 9$, $3^4 = 81 \equiv 13$, $3^8 \equiv 169 \equiv 16$; $3^{13} \equiv 16\cdot13\cdot3 = 624 \equiv 12 \pmod{17}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $3^1 = 3$, $3^2 = 9$, $3^4 = 81 \equiv 13$, $3^8 = 169 \equiv 16 \pmod{17}$. With $13 = 8 + 4 + 1$:
$3^{13} \equiv 16\cdot13\cdot3 = 624 = 36\cdot17 + 12 \equiv 12$. \emph{Check}: $3^{16} \equiv 1$ (Fermat), so $3^{13} \equiv 3^{-3} = 27^{-1} \equiv 10^{-1} \equiv 12$
since $10\cdot12 = 120 = 7\cdot17 + 1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $5 \equiv 3^5 \pmod{17}$ ($243 = 14\cdot17 + 5$); it uses the wrong exponent.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $3 = 3^1$ is the starting value; it would require $3^{12} \equiv 1$, but the order of $3$ modulo $17$ is $16$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $16 \equiv 3^8$ is only one of the three factors needed for $13 = 8 + 4 + 1$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Repeated squaring is the classical model for the controlled-$U^{2^j}$ structure of the quantum circuit.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{6}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Square-and-multiply cost}
Square-and-multiply computes $a^{1000} \bmod N$ from the binary expansion $1000 = 1111101000_2$. The number of modular multiplications
(squarings plus extra multiplications) is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$10$ & \optlabel{B}\,$16$ & \optlabel{C}\,$999$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$14$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $14$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Square-and-multiply performs one squaring per bit after the leading one and one extra multiplication per further $1$-bit.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $1000 = 1111101000_2$: $10$ bits $\Rightarrow 9$ squarings; six $1$-bits $\Rightarrow 5$ multiplications; total $14$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Left-to-right: start with $a$ (leading bit), then for each of the remaining $9$ bits square once ($9$ squarings) and multiply by $a$ when the bit is
1. The bits after the leading one are $111101000$: five 1s, so $5$ extra multiplications. Total $9 + 5 = 14$. Naively $999$ multiplications would be needed.
This is the classical idea behind computing $a^{2^j} \bmod N$ in Shor's circuit.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $10$ is the number of bits; it ignores the extra multiplications for the $1$-bits (and overcounts the squarings by one).
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $16$ counts a squaring and a multiplication for each of the six $1$-bits plus extras; only $9 + 5$ operations are needed.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $999$ multiplications is the naive method $a\cdot a\cdots a$, which is exponential in the bit length.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Modular exponentiation is polynomial: $O(n)$ multiplications of $n$-bit numbers, $O(n^3)$ bit operations.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{7}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Orders divide $\lambda(N)$}
For $N = 35$, which of the following can \emph{not} be the multiplicative order of any $a$ with $\gcd(a, 35) = 1$?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$6$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$5$ & \optlabel{C}\,$4$ & \optlabel{D}\,$12$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $5$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Every order divides the Carmichael function $\lambda(N)$, the exponent of the group $\mathbb Z_N^*$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\lambda(35) = \operatorname{lcm}(\lambda(5), \lambda(7)) = \operatorname{lcm}(4, 6) = 12$; possible orders are the divisors of $12$: $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} By the Chinese remainder theorem the order modulo $35$ is $\operatorname{lcm}(r_5, r_7)$ with $r_5 \mid 4$ and $r_7 \mid 6$, so every order divides the
Carmichael value $\lambda(35) = \operatorname{lcm}(4, 6) = 12$ (and $\varphi(35) = 24$). Orders $12$ (e.g.\ $a = 2$), $4$ (e.g.\ $a = 8$: $8^2 = 64 \equiv 29$,
$8^4 \equiv 1$) and $6$ (e.g.\ $a = 4$: $4^3 = 64 \equiv 29$, $4^6 \equiv 1$) occur; $5$ divides neither $12$ nor $24$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $6$ divides $12$ and is attained, e.g.\ by $a = 4$ ($4^3 = 64 \equiv 29 \not\equiv 1$, $4^6 \equiv 1$, $4^2 = 16$).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $4$ divides $12$ and is attained, e.g.\ by $a = 8$ ($8^2 = 64 \equiv 29$, $8^4 \equiv 29^2 = 841 \equiv 1$).
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $12 = \lambda(35)$ is attained, e.g.\ by $a = 3$ ($3^{12} \equiv 1$ and no smaller power is $1$).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Orders divide $\lambda(N)$, which divides $\varphi(N)$; $5$ does not divide $12$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{8}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Lucky gcd probability}
For $N = 15$, a base $a$ is drawn uniformly from $\{2, 3, \dots, 13\}$. The probability that $\gcd(a, 15) > 1$, so that a factor is found classically
without any quantum step, is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$1/2$ & \optlabel{B}\,$8/15$ & \optlabel{C}\,$7/15$ & \optlabel{D}\,$1/3$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $1/2$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Before any quantum step, Shor's algorithm computes $\gcd(a, N)$; if it exceeds $1$ a factor is found classically.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} In $\{2, \dots, 13\}$ (12 values) the bases sharing a factor with $15$ are $3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12$: $6/12 = 1/2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The multiples of 3 or 5 in $\{2, \dots, 13\}$ are $3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12$: six of the twelve values, probability $\frac12$. (For RSA-sized $N = pq$ this
probability is about $\frac1p + \frac1q$, astronomically small --- the lucky gcd is only an artefact of tiny examples.)

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $8/15 = \varphi(15)/15$ is the fraction of coprime residues in $\{0, \dots, 14\}$, the complement of what is asked, on the wrong set.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $7/15$ divides by all $15$ residues and counts $0$; the bases are drawn from $12$ values, $6$ of which are lucky.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $1/3$ counts only the multiples of $3$ ($3, 6, 9, 12$) or of $5$ separately; both kinds must be included.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} For tiny $N$ lucky bases are common; for RSA moduli the probability is negligible ($\approx 2/\sqrt N$).
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{9}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Chinese remainder theorem}
The unique $x \in \{0, \dots, 14\}$ with $x \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ and $x \equiv 3 \pmod 5$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$11$ & \optlabel{B}\,$2$ & \optlabel{C}\,$13$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$8$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $8$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The Chinese remainder theorem: for coprime moduli, the system has a unique solution modulo their product.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $x \equiv 3 \pmod 5$: $x \in \{3, 8, 13\}$; of these only $8 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Candidates with $x \equiv 3 \pmod 5$: $3, 8, 13$; their residues mod 3 are $0, 2, 1$. So $x = 8$. The Chinese remainder theorem guarantees one solution
modulo $15$; it is the reason why orders modulo $N = pq$ are least common multiples of the orders modulo $p$ and $q$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $11 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ but $11 \equiv 1 \pmod 5$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $2 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ but $2 \not\equiv 3 \pmod 5$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $13 \equiv 3 \pmod 5$ but $13 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, not $2$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} CRT explains the four square roots of $1$ modulo $pq$: $\pm1$ modulo each prime independently.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{10}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Square roots of $1$ mod $15$}
The complete set of solutions of $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{15}$ with $0 \le x < 15$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\{1, 11\}$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$\{1, 4, 11, 14\}$ & \optlabel{C}\,$\{1, 14\}$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\{1, 4, 14\}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $\{1, 4, 11, 14\}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Modulo $N = pq$, $x^2 \equiv 1$ iff $x \equiv \pm1$ modulo both $p$ and $q$ (CRT), giving four solutions.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $1^2 = 1$, $4^2 = 16 \equiv 1$, $11^2 = 121 \equiv 1$, $14^2 = 196 \equiv 1 \pmod{15}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} By CRT, $x^2 \equiv 1$ mod 15 iff $x \equiv \pm1 \pmod 3$ and $x \equiv \pm1 \pmod 5$: four combinations, $x = 1, 4, 11, 14$
($4^2 = 16$, $11^2 = 121 = 8\cdot15 + 1$). The non-trivial roots $4$ and $11$ give factors: $\gcd(4 - 1, 15) = 3$, $\gcd(4 + 1, 15) = 5$. Shor's algorithm
finds such a root as $x = a^{r/2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $\{1, 11\}$ misses $4$ and $14$; $14 \equiv -1$ is always a root.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $\{1, 14\}$ are only the trivial roots $\pm1$; the non-trivial ones $4$ and $11$ are what Shor's algorithm exploits.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $\{1, 4, 14\}$ misses $11 = 15 - 4$; roots come in pairs $\pm x$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} A non-trivial square root of $1$ immediately factors $N$ via $\gcd(x \pm 1, N)$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{11}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Failure: $a^{r/2} \equiv -1$}
For $N = 21$ and $a = 5$, the order $r$ and the outcome of Shor's classical reduction are
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] $r = 6$; the reduction fails because $5^3 \equiv -1 \pmod{21}$
\item[\optlabel{B}] $r = 3$; it fails because $r$ is odd
\item[\optlabel{C}] $r = 12$; it gives the factors $3$ and $7$
\item[\optlabel{D}] $r = 6$; it gives the factors $3$ and $7$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $r = 6$; the reduction fails because $5^3 \equiv -1 \pmod{21}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The reduction needs $r$ even and $a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1$; otherwise the attempt fails and a new base is chosen.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Powers of $5$ mod $21$: $5, 4, 20, 16, 17, 1$ $\Rightarrow r = 6$; $5^3 \equiv 20 \equiv -1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $5^1 = 5$, $5^2 = 25 \equiv 4$, $5^3 \equiv 20 \equiv -1$, $5^6 \equiv 1$: $r = 6$ (even). But $a^{r/2} = 5^3 \equiv -1$, so
$\gcd(5^3 + 1, 21) = \gcd(21, 21) = 21$ and $\gcd(5^3 - 1, 21) = \gcd(19, 21) = 1$: only trivial factors. The algorithm must restart with another $a$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $5^3 \equiv 20 \ne 1$, so $3$ is not the order; the order is $6$, which is even.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $12$ is a multiple of the order, not the order; $5^6 \equiv 1$ already.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] With $5^3 \equiv -1$ the gcds are $\gcd(19, 21) = 1$ and $\gcd(21, 21) = 21$: trivial, so no factors are obtained.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Correct order finding can still give a failed attempt; report it as a failure and retry.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{12}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Fermat's little theorem}
$2^{100} \bmod 13$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$9$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$3$ & \optlabel{D}\,$12$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $3$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Fermat's little theorem: $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ for prime $p \nmid a$; reduce the exponent modulo the order.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $2^{12} \equiv 1 \pmod{13}$, $100 = 8\cdot12 + 4$, so $2^{100} \equiv 2^4 = 16 \equiv 3$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Fermat: $2^{12} \equiv 1 \pmod{13}$. $100 = 8\cdot12 + 4$, so $2^{100} \equiv 2^4 = 16 \equiv 3$. Reducing the exponent modulo the order (or
$\varphi$) is what makes $a^x \bmod N$ periodic in $x$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $9 \equiv 2^8 \pmod{13}$ ($256 = 19\cdot13 + 9$): it reduces the exponent incorrectly; $100 \bmod 12 = 4$, not $8$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1$ would require $12 \mid 100$; $100 = 8\cdot12 + 4$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $12 \equiv -1$ is $2^6$; the exponent $100$ reduces to $4$, not $6$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Exponents can be reduced modulo the order --- which is exactly why the order is so useful.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{13}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Trial-division bound}
Trial division factors $N = 10403$ by testing divisors $d \ge 2$ in increasing order. The largest $d$ that may have to be tested is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$5201$ & \optlabel{B}\,$102$ & \optlabel{C}\,$103$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$101$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $101$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} A composite $N$ has a prime factor $\le \sqrt N$, so trial division stops at $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\sqrt{10403} = 101.99$; $10403 = 101\cdot103$, so $d = 101$ is reached and divides.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} If $N$ is composite it has a factor $\le\sqrt N$. $101^2 = 10201 \le 10403 < 102^2 = 10404$, so testing up to $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor = 101$ suffices
--- and $10403 = 101\times103$ is found at $d = 101$. For an $n$-bit $N$ this is about $2^{n/2}$ divisions: exponential in $n$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $5201 \approx N/2$ is a far too pessimistic bound; divisors above $\sqrt N$ pair with ones below it.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $102 > \sqrt{10403}$ is never needed (and is even); the search stops at $101$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $103$ is the larger factor; it is found as $N/101$, never by testing.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Trial division costs $O(\sqrt N) = O(2^{n/2})$ --- exponential in the bit length.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{14}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Success bound $1 - 2^{-(k-1)}$}
For an odd $N$ with $k$ distinct prime factors (not a prime power) and $a$ uniformly random among the residues coprime to $N$, the probability
that $r$ is even and $a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 \pmod N$ is at least $1 - 2^{-(k-1)}$. For $N = 105 = 3\cdot5\cdot7$ this lower bound is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$1/8$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1/2$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$3/4$ & \optlabel{D}\,$7/8$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $3/4$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} For $N$ with $k$ distinct odd prime factors, a random coprime base works with probability at least $1 - 2^{-(k-1)}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $k = 3$: $1 - 2^{-2} = 3/4$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $k = 3$: $1 - 2^{-2} = \frac34$. For RSA moduli ($k = 2$) the bound is $\frac12$, so on average at most two bases are needed. This bound comes from
the CRT: the reduction fails only if the 2-adic parts of the orders modulo the prime powers all agree.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1/8 = 2^{-3}$ confuses the failure bound with the success bound and uses the wrong exponent.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1/2$ is the bound for $k = 2$ (an RSA modulus), not for three prime factors.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $7/8 = 1 - 2^{-3}$ uses the exponent $k$ instead of $k - 1$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} For an RSA modulus at least half of the bases work, so a few repetitions suffice.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{15}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{$\varphi$, order, $\lambda$, inverse}
Match each quantity for $N = 15$ (List-I) with its value (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $\varphi(15)$ & \textbf{(1)} & $13$ \\
\textbf{(Q)} & order of $4$ modulo $15$ & \textbf{(2)} & $8$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & Carmichael value $\lambda(15) = \operatorname{lcm}(\lambda(3), \lambda(5))$ & \textbf{(3)} & $2$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & $7^{-1} \bmod 15$ & \textbf{(4)} & $4$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$2, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$4 \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$3, R$\to$4, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$3, S$\to$1
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} P$\to$2, Q$\to$3, R$\to$4, S$\to$1

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} $\varphi$, $\lambda$, orders and inverses are basic invariants of $\mathbb Z_N^*$; for $N = 15$ they can be computed by hand.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\varphi(15) = 2\cdot4 = 8$; $4^2 = 16 \equiv 1$ so $\operatorname{ord}(4) = 2$; $\lambda(15) = \operatorname{lcm}(2, 4) = 4$; $7\cdot13 = 91 \equiv 1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item $\varphi(15) = 2\cdot4 = 8$ (2).
\item $4^2 = 16 \equiv 1$: order $2$ (3).
\item $\lambda(15) = \operatorname{lcm}(2, 4) = 4$ (4): every order divides it.
\item $7\cdot13 = 91 = 6\cdot15 + 1$: $7^{-1} = 13$ (1).
\end{itemize}
Hence P$\to$2, Q$\to$3, R$\to$4, S$\to$1.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] This assigns $4$ to $\varphi(15)$; $\varphi(15) = 8$ counts $1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] This gives $\lambda(15) = 13$ and $7^{-1} = 4$; but $7\cdot4 = 28 \equiv 13 \not\equiv 1$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] This swaps the order of $4$ and $\lambda(15)$: $4^2 \equiv 1$, so the order is $2$, while $\lambda(15) = 4$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Orders divide $\lambda(N)$, which divides $\varphi(N)$: here $2 \mid 4 \mid 8$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{16}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Classical factoring complexity}
Match each classical algorithm (List-I) with its running time for an $n$-bit input $N$ (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & trial division & \textbf{(1)} & $\exp\big((64/9)^{1/3}(\ln N)^{1/3}(\ln\ln N)^{2/3}(1 + o(1))\big)$ (sub-exponential) \\
\textbf{(Q)} & Pollard's rho & \textbf{(2)} & $O(N^{1/4})$ expected, i.e.\ $O(2^{n/4})$ (heuristic) \\
\textbf{(R)} & general number field sieve & \textbf{(3)} & $O(n)$ division steps (polynomial) \\
\textbf{(S)} & Euclidean $\gcd(a, N)$ & \textbf{(4)} & $O(\sqrt N) = O(2^{n/2})$ divisions \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$1, R$\to$2, S$\to$3 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$3, S$\to$1 & \correctlabel{D}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$1, S$\to$3
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$1, S$\to$3

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Classical factoring methods range from exponential (trial division, rho) to sub-exponential (GNFS); gcd is polynomial.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Trial division $O(2^{n/2})$; Pollard rho $O(2^{n/4})$; GNFS $L_N[1/3, (64/9)^{1/3}]$; Euclid $O(n)$ steps.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item trial division tests divisors up to $\sqrt N$ (4);
\item Pollard's rho finds a factor $p$ in about $\sqrt p \le N^{1/4}$ steps (2);
\item the GNFS is the fastest known general method, sub-exponential but super-polynomial (1);
\item the gcd is polynomial (3) --- not a factoring algorithm on its own.
\end{itemize}
Hence P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$1, S$\to$3. Not all classical factoring is exponential.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] This swaps trial division and Pollard's rho; rho finds a factor $p$ in about $\sqrt p \le N^{1/4}$ steps, faster than trial division.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] This gives Pollard's rho the GNFS running time and vice versa; GNFS is the fastest known general method.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] This gives the gcd the GNFS time; the Euclidean algorithm is polynomial, $O(n)$ division steps.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The best classical method is sub-exponential; Shor's algorithm is polynomial --- on a fault-tolerant machine.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{17}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Non-trivial square root $\Rightarrow$ factor}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} If $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod N$ but $x \not\equiv \pm1 \pmod N$, then $\gcd(x - 1, N)$ is a non-trivial factor of $N$.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} In that case $N$ divides $(x - 1)(x + 1)$ but divides neither $x - 1$ nor $x + 1$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} If $N \mid (x - 1)(x + 1)$ but $N$ divides neither factor, each prime factor of $N$ is split between them.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $x^2 \equiv 1 \Rightarrow N \mid (x - 1)(x + 1)$; $x \not\equiv \pm1 \Rightarrow 1 < \gcd(x \pm 1, N) < N$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{R is true}: $x^2 - 1 = (x-1)(x+1) \equiv 0$, while $x \not\equiv \pm1$ means $N \nmid x \mp 1$. \textbf{A follows from R}: if $\gcd(x - 1, N)$ were
$1$, then $N \mid (x-1)(x+1)$ would force $N \mid x + 1$; if it were $N$, then $N \mid x - 1$ --- both excluded. So it is a proper divisor. This is exactly
Shor's factor-extraction step with $x = a^{r/2}$. Answer: (A).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] is wrong because R is exactly the argument that proves A: a divisor of a product that divides neither factor must share a proper factor with each.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] is wrong because R is true: $x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) \equiv 0$, and $x \not\equiv \pm1$ means $N$ divides neither factor.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] is wrong because A is true: e.g.\ $x = 4$, $N = 15$ gives $\gcd(3, 15) = 3$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} This is the heart of the reduction: $x = a^{r/2}$ is a square root of $1$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{18}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Euler's theorem vs order}
\textbf{Statement I:} If $\gcd(a, N) = 1$, then $a^{\varphi(N)} \equiv 1 \pmod N$.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} The multiplicative order of every $a$ coprime to $N$ equals $\varphi(N)$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\correctlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} Statement I is true, but Statement II is false

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Euler's theorem gives an exponent that always works; the order is the smallest one and is usually a proper divisor of $\varphi(N)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $a^{\varphi(N)} \equiv 1$; $\operatorname{ord}(a) \mid \lambda(N) \mid \varphi(N)$; e.g.\ $\operatorname{ord}_{15}(4) = 2 \ne 8$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is true} (Euler's theorem). \textbf{II is false}: the order only \emph{divides} $\varphi(N)$; e.g.\ $4$ has order $2$ modulo $15$ while
$\varphi(15) = 8$. Finding the actual order is the hard problem that Shor's quantum period finding solves. Answer: (C).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] is wrong because Statement II is false: $\operatorname{ord}_{15}(4) = 2$ while $\varphi(15) = 8$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] is wrong because Statement I is Euler's theorem, which holds for every $a$ coprime to $N$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] is wrong because Statement I is true and Statement II false, not the other way round.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} If orders were always $\varphi(N)$, knowing them would directly reveal $\varphi(N)$; in reality they only divide it.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 19 and 20}
Shor's reduction is applied by hand to $N = 91 = 7\times13$ with the base $a = 3$ (note $\gcd(3, 91) = 1$). Recall that the
order $r$ of $a$ modulo $N$ is the least $r > 0$ with $a^r \equiv 1 \pmod N$, and that if $r$ is even and $a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 \pmod N$,
then $\gcd(a^{r/2} \pm 1, N)$ are non-trivial factors.
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{19}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Order of $3$ mod $91$}
The order $r$ of $3$ modulo $91$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$72$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$6$ & \optlabel{C}\,$12$ & \optlabel{D}\,$3$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $6$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The order is the first exponent where the powers return to $1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $3, 9, 27, 81, 243 \equiv 61, 183 \equiv 1 \pmod{91}$ ($729 = 8\cdot91 + 1$): $r = 6$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} By CRT, $r = \operatorname{lcm}(r_7, r_{13})$. Mod 7: $3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1$: order $6$. Mod 13: $3, 9, 27 \equiv 1$: order $3$. So $r = \operatorname{lcm}(6, 3) = 6$.
\emph{Check}: $3^6 = 729 = 8\cdot91 + 1$. ($72 = \varphi(91)$ is only a multiple of the order.)

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $72 = \varphi(91)$ is an exponent that works, not the least one.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $12$ is a multiple of the order ($3^{12} \equiv 1$) but not the least one.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $3^3 = 27 \ne 1$; $3$ is half of the order.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Order $=$ smallest exponent; multiples and $\varphi(N)$ also satisfy $a^x \equiv 1$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{20}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Factors of $91$ by gcd}
The values of $\gcd(3^{r/2} - 1, 91)$ and $\gcd(3^{r/2} + 1, 91)$ are, respectively,
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$26$ and $28$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1$ and $91$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$13$ and $7$ & \optlabel{D}\,$7$ and $13$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $13$ and $7$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} With $r$ even and $a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1$, the gcds with $a^{r/2} \mp 1$ give the factors.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $3^{r/2} = 27$; $\gcd(26, 91) = 13$, $\gcd(28, 91) = 7$; $7\cdot13 = 91$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $r = 6$ is even and $3^3 = 27 \not\equiv -1 \equiv 90$. $\gcd(26, 91) = 13$ (since $91 = 7\cdot13$, $26 = 2\cdot13$) and $\gcd(28, 91) = 7$
($28 = 4\cdot7$). Both factors are found: $91 = 7\times13$. The order of the two numbers matters: $a^{r/2} - 1 = 26$ shares $13$ with $91$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $26$ and $28$ are $a^{r/2} \mp 1$ themselves; the gcd with $91$ is still needed.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1$ and $91$ would be the trivial result for $a^{r/2} \equiv -1$; but $27 \not\equiv 90$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $7$ and $13$ are the correct factors in the wrong order: $\gcd(26, 91) = 13$ and $\gcd(28, 91) = 7$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The quantum part ends with $r$; the factors come from two classical gcds.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\newpage

\begin{sectionbanner}SECTION B \enspace$\cdot$\enspace Quantum Computing Foundations \hfill Q.21--40\end{sectionbanner}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{21}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Uniform superposition}
After $H^{\otimes8}$ acts on $\ket{0}^{\otimes8}$ (the counting register of the notebook for $N = 15$), the amplitude of each basis state $\ket x$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$1/256$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$1/16$ & \optlabel{C}\,$1/8$ & \optlabel{D}\,$1/\sqrt8$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $1/16$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The Hadamard transform of $\ket0^{\otimes t}$ is the uniform superposition of all $2^t$ basis states.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $H^{\otimes t}\ket0^{\otimes t} = 2^{-t/2}\sum_x\ket x$; $t = 8$: amplitude $1/16$, probability $1/256$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $H^{\otimes t}\ket{0}^{\otimes t} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^t}}\sum_{x=0}^{2^t-1}\ket x$. With $t = 8$: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{256}} = \frac1{16}$. The probabilities are $\frac{1}{256}$ each.
This superposition is the input on which the modular exponentiation acts ``for all $x$ at once''.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1/256$ is the probability $|1/16|^2$, not the amplitude.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $1/8$ would be the amplitude for $t = 6$ ($2^{-3}$); for $t = 8$ it is $2^{-4}$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $1/\sqrt8$ is the amplitude for $t = 3$ qubits.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Amplitudes are $2^{-t/2}$; probabilities $2^{-t}$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{22}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Measuring the work register}
The state $\frac{1}{\sqrt8}\sum_{x=0}^{7}\ket x\ket{2^x \bmod 15}$ is prepared and the \emph{second} register is measured with result $4$. The probability
of this result and the post-measurement state of the first register are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$1/2$; $\ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket2 + \ket6)$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1/4$; $\ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket2 - \ket6)$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$1/8$; $\ \ket2$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$1/4$; $\ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket2 + \ket6)$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $1/4$; $\ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket2 + \ket6)$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Measuring one register of an entangled state keeps only the compatible terms of the other, renormalised.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $2^x \bmod 15$: $1, 2, 4, 8, 1, 2, 4, 8$; value $4$ at $x = 2, 6$: $P = 2/8$, state $(\ket2 + \ket6)/\sqrt2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $2^x \bmod 15$ for $x = 0, \dots, 7$: $1, 2, 4, 8, 1, 2, 4, 8$. The value $4$ occurs for $x = 2$ and $x = 6$, so
$P = 2\times\frac18 = \frac14$, and the first register collapses to $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket2 + \ket6)$ (equal positive amplitudes, renormalised). It is periodic
with period $r = 4$ and an unknown offset --- the QFT removes the offset from the probabilities.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1/2$ counts two of the four values as matching; only $x = 2, 6$ of $8$ terms give $4$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The amplitudes before the measurement are all $+1/\sqrt8$; no minus sign can appear.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $1/8$ and $\ket2$ forget that the function is periodic: $x = 6$ gives $2^6 = 64 \equiv 4$ as well.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The collapsed first register is periodic with period $r$ and a random offset.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{23}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Unitarity of $U_a$}
Why does the operator $U_a\ket y = \ket{ay \bmod N}$ (for $0 \le y < N$; identity for $y \ge N$) require $\gcd(a, N) = 1$ to be a valid quantum gate?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] because the eigenvalues of $U_a$ must be real
\item[\optlabel{B}] because a quantum gate must map $\ket0$ to $\ket0$
\item[\correctlabel{C}] only then is $y \mapsto ay \bmod N$ a permutation of $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, so $U_a$ is a permutation matrix and hence unitary
\item[\optlabel{D}] because otherwise $U_a$ would not be Hermitian
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} only then is $y \mapsto ay \bmod N$ a permutation of $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, so $U_a$ is a permutation matrix and hence unitary

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} A permutation matrix is unitary; a non-injective map of basis states is not.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\gcd(a, N) = 1 \iff a$ invertible mod $N \iff y \mapsto ay \bmod N$ bijective on $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} If $\gcd(a, N) = d > 1$, two inputs collide: e.g.\ $a = 3$, $N = 15$: $3\cdot0 \equiv 3\cdot5 \equiv 0$. A non-injective map cannot be unitary.
For $\gcd(a, N) = 1$, $a$ is invertible modulo $N$, the map is a bijection, and a permutation matrix satisfies $U^\dagger U = I$. Gates need not be
Hermitian, and their eigenvalues are complex phases.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Unitary eigenvalues are phases $e^{i\phi}$; $U_a$ has complex eigenvalues $e^{2\pi is/r}$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Gates need not fix $\ket0$; $U_a$ happens to fix $\ket0$, but that is not the requirement.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Quantum gates must be unitary, not Hermitian; $U_a$ is generally not Hermitian (it cycles states).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Coprimality makes modular multiplication reversible, hence implementable as a quantum gate.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{24}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Eigenvalues of $U_a$}
On the subspace spanned by $\{\ket1, \ket2, \ket4, \ket8\}$, the operator $U_2\ket y = \ket{2y \bmod 15}$ has the eigenvalues
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$1, 2, 4, 8$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1, -1$ (each twice) \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$e^{2\pi i/15}, e^{4\pi i/15}, e^{8\pi i/15}, e^{16\pi i/15}$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$1, i, -1, -i$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $1, i, -1, -i$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} A cyclic permutation of length $r$ has the $r$-th roots of unity as eigenvalues.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $U_2$: $1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 8 \to 1$, $r = 4$; eigenvalues $e^{2\pi is/4} = 1, i, -1, -i$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $U_2$ cycles $\ket1 \to \ket2 \to \ket4 \to \ket8 \to \ket1$: a cyclic shift of length $r = 4$, so $U_2^4 = I$ there and the eigenvalues are the fourth
roots of unity $e^{2\pi is/4}$, $s = 0, 1, 2, 3$. In general the eigenvalues on the orbit of $\ket1$ are $e^{2\pi is/r}$: the order $r$ is encoded in the
eigenphases $s/r$ --- this is what phase estimation reads out.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1, 2, 4, 8$ are the basis labels on the orbit, not eigenvalues; unitary eigenvalues have modulus $1$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\pm1$ would require $U_2^2 = I$, but $U_2^2\ket1 = \ket4 \ne \ket1$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Phases with denominator $15$ use $N$ instead of the order $r = 4$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The order is hidden in the eigenphases $s/r$ of $U_a$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{25}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$\ket1$ as sum of eigenvectors}
With $\ket{u_s} = \frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}e^{-2\pi isk/r}\ket{a^k \bmod N}$, the superposition $\frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{s=0}^{r-1}\ket{u_s}$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\ket a$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$\ket1$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$\ket0$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{y=0}^{N-1}\ket y$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $\ket1$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The eigenvectors $\ket{u_s}$ are Fourier transforms of the orbit; summing over $s$ inverts the transform.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\sum_{s=0}^{r-1}e^{-2\pi isk/r} = r\,\delta_{k,0}$, so $\frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_s\ket{u_s} = \ket{a^0} = \ket1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_s\ket{u_s} = \frac1r\sum_k\Big(\sum_se^{-2\pi isk/r}\Big)\ket{a^k} = \sum_k\delta_{k,0}\ket{a^k} = \ket{a^0} = \ket1$, because the sum of
$r$-th roots of unity vanishes unless $k \equiv 0$. That is why the work register is initialised to $\ket1$: it is an equal superposition of all eigenvectors,
and QPE returns a random $s/r$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $\ket a = \ket{a^1}$ would need the phase factors $e^{2\pi is/r}$ inserted before summing.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $\ket0$ is outside the orbit $\{a^k \bmod N\}$ of $\ket1$, so it cannot be a combination of the $\ket{u_s}$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] The uniform superposition over all residues is not in the span of one orbit (it includes non-coprime values).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Initialising the work register to $\ket1$ prepares all eigenvectors at once, so QPE yields a random $s/r$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{26}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Phase kickback}
A control qubit in $\ket+$ controls a unitary $U$ acting on its eigenvector $\ket u$, $U\ket u = e^{i\phi}\ket u$, with $\phi = 2\pi/3$. Afterwards, the
expectation value $\langle X\rangle$ of the control qubit is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$1/2$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1$ & \optlabel{C}\,$-\sqrt3/2$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$-1/2$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $-1/2$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Phase kickback moves the eigenphase of the target onto the $\ket1$ branch of the control.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\ket+\ket u \mapsto \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + e^{i\phi}\ket1)\ket u$; $\langle X\rangle = \cos\phi$, $\langle Y\rangle = \sin\phi$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Phase kickback: $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + \ket1)\ket u \mapsto \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + e^{i\phi}\ket1)\ket u$ --- the work register is unchanged, the phase moves to
the control. For $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + e^{i\phi}\ket1)$, $\langle X\rangle = \cos\phi = \cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = -\frac12$ (and $\langle Y\rangle = \sin\phi = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}$).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1/2 = \cos(\pi/3)$ uses half of the phase.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\langle X\rangle = 1$ is the value before the controlled gate; the kickback rotates the state.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $-\sqrt3/2$ mixes up sine and cosine; $\sin(2\pi/3) = +\sqrt3/2$ is $\langle Y\rangle$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The control qubit records the phase; the eigenvector target is untouched.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{27}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Phases of $U^{2^j}$}
In phase estimation, counting qubit $j$ controls $U^{2^j}$. If $U\ket u = e^{2\pi i/6}\ket u$, the phase kicked back onto counting qubit $j = 2$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$2\pi$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\pi/3$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$4\pi/3$ & \optlabel{D}\,$2\pi/3$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $4\pi/3$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Applying $U^{2^j}$ to an eigenvector multiplies its phase by $2^j$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Phase on qubit $j$: $2\pi\varphi\cdot2^j$; $\varphi = 1/6$, $j = 2$: $2\pi\cdot4/6 = 4\pi/3$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $U^{2^j}\ket u = e^{2\pi i\cdot2^j/6}\ket u$; for $j = 2$: $2\pi\cdot\frac46 = \frac{4\pi}{3}$ (equivalently $-\frac{2\pi}{3}$). Each counting qubit receives the phase
doubled relative to the previous one --- the binary-fraction pattern that the inverse QFT decodes.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $2\pi$ would correspond to $U^6$; $2^j = 4$, not $6$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\pi/3 = 2\pi/6$ is the phase for $j = 0$ ($U$ itself).
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $2\pi/3$ is the phase for $j = 1$ ($U^2$).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Counting qubit $j$ carries the binary digit pattern $2^j\varphi \bmod 1$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{28}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Hadamard transform signs}
$(H\otimes H)\ket{11}$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$\frac12(\ket{00} - \ket{01} - \ket{10} + \ket{11})$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} - \ket{11})$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$\frac12(\ket{00} - \ket{01} - \ket{10} - \ket{11})$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\frac12(\ket{00} + \ket{01} + \ket{10} + \ket{11})$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $\frac12(\ket{00} - \ket{01} - \ket{10} + \ket{11})$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} $H^{\otimes n}\ket x = 2^{-n/2}\sum_y(-1)^{x\cdot y}\ket y$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $x = 11$: signs $(-1)^{y_1 + y_2}$: $+, -, -, +$ for $00, 01, 10, 11$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $H\ket1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 - \ket1)$, so $H\ket1\otimes H\ket1 = \frac12(\ket0 - \ket1)(\ket0 - \ket1) = \frac12(\ket{00} - \ket{01} - \ket{10} + \ket{11})$.
In general $H^{\otimes n}\ket x = 2^{-n/2}\sum_y(-1)^{x\cdot y}\ket y$: signs depend on the parity of $x\cdot y$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] A Bell-type state cannot arise from local Hadamards on a product state.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The last sign is $(-1)^{1 + 1} = +1$, not $-1$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] All plus signs is $(H\otimes H)\ket{00}$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Hadamard transforms encode parities in signs --- the simplest Fourier transform.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{29}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Two-path interference}
Two computational paths lead to the same outcome with amplitudes $\frac12$ and $\frac12e^{i\theta}$. For $\theta = 2\pi/3$ the probability of that outcome is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1/2$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$1/4$ & \optlabel{D}\,$3/4$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $1/4$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Probabilities come from the squared modulus of the \emph{sum} of amplitudes of indistinguishable paths.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\big|\frac12(1 + e^{i\theta})\big|^2 = \cos^2(\theta/2)$; $\theta = 2\pi/3$: $\cos^2(\pi/3) = 1/4$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Amplitudes add before squaring: $\big|\frac12(1 + e^{i\theta})\big|^2 = \frac14|1 + e^{i\theta}|^2 = \frac14(2 + 2\cos\theta) = \cos^2\frac\theta2 = \cos^2\frac\pi3 = \frac14$.
Interference concentrates probability where the phases agree; in Shor's algorithm the inverse QFT arranges this for $y \approx k2^t/r$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0$ needs $\theta = \pi$ (complete destructive interference).
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1/2$ adds probabilities ($\frac14 + \frac14$) instead of amplitudes, ignoring interference.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $3/4 = \sin^2(\pi/3)$ is the probability of the other output port.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Interference, not parallelism alone, makes the right answer likely.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{30}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Reversible modular exponentiation}
Why does Shor's circuit compute $\ket x\ket1 \mapsto \ket x\ket{a^x \bmod N}$ instead of $\ket x \mapsto \ket{a^x \bmod N}$ in place?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] the map $x \mapsto a^x \bmod N$ is not injective ($x$ and $x + r$ give the same value), so it cannot be a unitary on a single register; keeping $x$ makes it reversible
\item[\optlabel{B}] because a single register cannot hold numbers larger than $N$
\item[\optlabel{C}] because the Hadamard gates must act on a different register than the QFT
\item[\optlabel{D}] because measurement requires two registers
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} the map $x \mapsto a^x \bmod N$ is not injective ($x$ and $x + r$ give the same value), so it cannot be a unitary on a single register; keeping $x$ makes it reversible

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Unitary operations are invertible; a many-to-one function must keep its input to be reversible.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $a^{x + r} \equiv a^x$; $\ket x\ket y \mapsto \ket x\ket{y\,a^x \bmod N}$ is reversible.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Quantum gates are unitary, hence invertible. Since $a^{x + r} \equiv a^x$, an in-place map would send different inputs to the same output. Keeping the input
$x$ and writing the result into a second register (here by multiplying the work register $\ket1$ by $a^x$) gives a reversible map and entangles the
registers: $\sum_x\ket x\ket{a^x \bmod N}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Register size is not the issue: $a^x \bmod N < N$ always fits in $n$ qubits.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The Hadamards and the QFT both act on the counting register; this is not why two registers are used.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Measurement can be performed on any register; it does not require a second one.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Reversibility forces the input to be kept, which entangles the two registers.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{31}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{CNOT cost of a Fredkin gate}
A controlled-SWAP (Fredkin) gate is compiled as $\mathrm{CNOT}_{b\to a}\cdot\mathrm{Toffoli}_{c,a\to b}\cdot\mathrm{CNOT}_{b\to a}$, and each Toffoli uses the
standard decomposition with 6 CNOTs. The number of CNOTs per controlled-SWAP is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$9$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$8$ & \optlabel{C}\,$3$ & \optlabel{D}\,$6$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $8$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} A Fredkin gate can be built from two CNOTs around a Toffoli; a Toffoli needs 6 CNOTs in the standard decomposition.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathrm{CSWAP}_{c;a,b} = \mathrm{CX}_{b\to a}\,\mathrm{CCX}_{c,a\to b}\,\mathrm{CX}_{b\to a}$: $1 + 6 + 1 = 8$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $1 + 6 + 1 = 8$ CNOTs (plus single-qubit $H$, $T$, $T^\dagger$ gates). A plain SWAP needs $3$ CNOTs, but the control turns the middle CNOT into a Toffoli.
Gate-level modular multipliers are built from many such gates, which is why compiled Shor circuits are much larger than the notebook's matrix gates.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $9 = 3\times3$ treats every CNOT of a SWAP as a 3-CNOT gate; only the middle CNOT must become a (6-CNOT) Toffoli.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $3$ CNOTs make an uncontrolled SWAP; the control requires the Toffoli.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $6$ counts only the Toffoli and forgets the two outer CNOTs.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Controlled arithmetic is costly: every controlled SWAP is a Toffoli plus two CNOTs.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{32}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Implicit measurement}
\texttt{Shor.ipynb} measures only the counting register. Compared with also measuring the work register first, the distribution of the counting
outcome $y$ is
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] different: the peaks become twice as wide
\item[\optlabel{B}] undefined, because entangled registers cannot be measured separately
\item[\correctlabel{C}] exactly the same: a measurement of the other register that is never used cannot change the marginal statistics of $y$
\item[\optlabel{D}] different: without measuring the work register no periodic structure appears
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} exactly the same: a measurement of the other register that is never used cannot change the marginal statistics of $y$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Measuring a subsystem that is never used again does not change the reduced state of the rest.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\rho_{\text{count}} = \operatorname{Tr}_{\text{work}}\ket\Psi\!\bra\Psi = \sum_wP(w)\rho_{\text{count}|w}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The work register is not acted on after the controlled multiplications. Measuring it (or not) only changes which conditional state the counting
register is in; averaged over the unseen result, the reduced state of the counting register --- and hence $P(y)$ --- is identical (principle of implicit
measurement). Textbook derivations ``measure the second register'' only to simplify the algebra.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Peak widths depend on $t$ and $r$, not on whether the idle work register is measured.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Entangled registers can be measured separately; the marginal statistics are well defined.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] The periodic structure is in the entangled state already; the measurement of the work register only simplifies textbook algebra.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Principle of implicit (deferred) measurement: unused registers may be measured or ignored.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{33}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Notebook qubit count}
In \texttt{Shor.ipynb} the work register has $n = $ \texttt{N.bit\_length()} qubits and the counting register $t = 2n$. The total number of qubits for
$N = 143$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$24$ & \optlabel{B}\,$21$ & \optlabel{C}\,$22$ & \optlabel{D}\,$16$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $24$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The notebook uses $n = \lceil\log_2(N + 1)\rceil$ work qubits and $t = 2n$ counting qubits: $3n$ in total.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $143 = 10001111_2$: $n = 8$, $3n = 24$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $143 = 10001111_2$ has $8$ bits, so $n = 8$, $t = 16$ and $t + n = 24$ (the notebook's comment lists ``143 -> 24''). $16$ forgets the work register;
$22 = 2\lceil\log_2 143\rceil + 6$ has no basis.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $21$ would be $3\cdot7$, but $143 > 127 = 2^7 - 1$ needs $8$ bits.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $22$ does not follow from $t = 2n$ with $n = 8$; no formula of the notebook gives it.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $16$ is only the counting register $t = 2n$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Qubits scale as $3n$ here: three per bit of $N$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{34}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{State-vector memory}
The memory of a double-precision state vector (16 bytes per amplitude) for the 24-qubit circuit of the previous question is about
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$16.8$ MB & \optlabel{B}\,$384$ bytes & \optlabel{C}\,$4.3$ GB & \correctlabel{D}\,$268$ MB
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $268$ MB

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} A state vector of $q$ qubits has $2^q$ complex amplitudes of $16$ bytes (complex128).

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $M = 16\cdot2^q$ bytes; $q = 24$: $268\,435\,456$ B $\approx 268$ MB.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $16\times2^{24} = 268\,435\,456$ bytes $\approx 268$ MB (the notebook's table). $384 = 16\times24$ is linear; $16.8$ MB is $2^{20}\times16$ (20 qubits);
$4.3$ GB corresponds to 28 qubits. Each extra bit of $N$ adds 3 qubits, i.e.\ multiplies the memory by 8.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $16.8$ MB is $16\cdot2^{20}$, the memory of $20$ qubits.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $384$ bytes grows linearly with the number of qubits; state vectors grow exponentially.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $4.3$ GB is $16\cdot2^{28}$, the memory of $28$ qubits.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Each extra qubit doubles the memory; each extra bit of $N$ multiplies it by $8$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{35}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Roles of circuit blocks}
Match each operation of the order-finding circuit (List-I) with its role (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $H$ on every counting qubit & \textbf{(1)} & turns the phases $2\pi\cdot2^js/r$ into a binary estimate $y \approx 2^ts/r$ \\
\textbf{(Q)} & controlled $U_{a^{2^j} \bmod N}$ & \textbf{(2)} & prepares the work register in $\ket1$, an equal superposition of the eigenvectors $\ket{u_s}$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & inverse QFT on the counting register & \textbf{(3)} & creates the uniform superposition over all exponents $x$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & $X$ on the last work qubit & \textbf{(4)} & performs modular exponentiation / kicks the eigenphases back onto the counting qubits \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$2 & \correctlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$2
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Order finding: superposition, controlled modular exponentiation (kickback), inverse QFT, measurement.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^t}}\sum_x\ket x\ket1 \to \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^t}}\sum_x\ket x\ket{a^x} \to$ peaks at $y \approx k2^t/r$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item Hadamards: superposition over $x$ (3);
\item controlled powers of $U_a$: $\ket x\ket1 \mapsto \ket x\ket{a^x}$, equivalently phase kickback (4);
\item inverse QFT: interference that converts the periodic phase pattern into peaks at $y \approx k2^t/r$ (1);
\item $X$ on the least significant work qubit: $\ket{0001} = \ket1$ (2).
\end{itemize}
Hence P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] This gives the controlled multiplications the decoding role of the inverse QFT and the QFT the exponentiation.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] This swaps the roles of the inverse QFT and the $X$ gate; $X$ only prepares $\ket1$ in the work register.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] This gives the Hadamards the role of modular exponentiation and vice versa; the Hadamards only create the superposition.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Know what each block does: it is the basis for every resource and error discussion.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{36}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Phase gates $R_1(\lambda)$}
The phase gate is $R_1(\lambda) = \operatorname{diag}(1, e^{i\lambda})$ (controlled versions appear in the QFT). Match each angle (List-I) with the named gate (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $R_1(\pi)$ & \textbf{(1)} & $S^\dagger$ \\
\textbf{(Q)} & $R_1(\pi/2)$ & \textbf{(2)} & $T$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & $R_1(\pi/4)$ & \textbf{(3)} & $Z$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & $R_1(-\pi/2)$ & \textbf{(4)} & $S$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \correctlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$2, R$\to$4, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$2, S$\to$1
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} $R_1(\lambda) = \operatorname{diag}(1, e^{i\lambda})$ contains $Z$, $S$, $T$ and their inverses as special cases.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $e^{i\pi} = -1$, $e^{i\pi/2} = i$, $e^{i\pi/4}$, $e^{-i\pi/2} = -i$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $R_1(\pi) = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1) = Z$ (3); $R_1(\pi/2) = \operatorname{diag}(1, i) = S$ (4); $R_1(\pi/4) = \operatorname{diag}(1, e^{i\pi/4}) = T$ (2);
$R_1(-\pi/2) = \operatorname{diag}(1, -i) = S^\dagger$ (1). The inverse QFT of the notebook uses \texttt{cr1(-pi/2**(k-j))}: controlled $S^\dagger$, $T^\dagger$, \dots

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] This exchanges $T$ and $S^\dagger$; $R_1(-\pi/2)$ has $-i$ on the diagonal, which is $S^\dagger$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] This exchanges $S$ and $T$: $R_1(\pi/2) = \operatorname{diag}(1, i) = S$, while $T$ has $e^{i\pi/4}$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] This assigns $R_1(\pi)$ to $S$; $R_1(\pi) = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1) = Z$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The inverse QFT uses controlled $R_1(-\pi/2^k)$: controlled $S^\dagger$, $T^\dagger$ and finer rotations.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{37}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Kickback and controls}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} When the target register is in an eigenvector of $U$, a controlled-$U$ gate leaves the target register unchanged.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} Controlled gates never change the state of their control qubit.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\correctlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} A is true, but R is false

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Phase kickback: a controlled-$U$ on an eigenvector changes the control (in superposition), not the target.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $(\alpha\ket0 + \beta\ket1)\ket u \mapsto (\alpha\ket0 + \beta e^{i\phi}\ket1)\ket u$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{A is true}: $\ket c\ket u \mapsto \ket c\,e^{ic\phi}\ket u$ --- the target stays $\ket u$, only a phase appears. \textbf{R is false}: that phase belongs to the
control branch $\ket1$, so a control in superposition changes, $\ket+ \mapsto \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + e^{i\phi}\ket1)$ (phase kickback). This is precisely how
phase estimation and Shor's algorithm extract information. Answer: (C).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] is wrong because R is false: the control's relative phase changes, as phase kickback shows.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] is wrong for the same reason: R is false, so it cannot be true but irrelevant.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] is wrong because A is true: the target remains the eigenvector $\ket u$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} In QPE the information flows from target to control --- the opposite of the classical intuition.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{38}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Parallelism vs interference}
\textbf{Statement I:} Because the circuit evaluates $a^x \bmod N$ for all $x$ in superposition, measuring the registers directly reveals the period $r$.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} Interference produced by the inverse QFT is needed to turn the periodic structure into high-probability measurement outcomes.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\optlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\correctlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} Statement I is false, but Statement II is true

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Quantum parallelism produces a superposition, but a measurement returns one sample; interference extracts global properties.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Measuring $\sum_x\ket x\ket{f(x)}$ gives one pair $(x, f(x))$; the inverse QFT concentrates amplitude at $y \approx k2^t/r$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is false}: a measurement returns one random $x$ and one value $a^x \bmod N$ --- no more information than a single classical evaluation. Quantum
parallelism alone does not solve factoring. \textbf{II is true}: the inverse QFT makes the amplitudes interfere constructively near $y = k2^t/r$, so that one
measurement carries information about $r$. Answer: (D).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] is wrong because Statement I is false: a direct measurement yields one random evaluation, not the period.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] is wrong because Statement II is true: interference via the inverse QFT is the essential step.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] has the truth values reversed: I is false and II is true.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Parallelism alone does not solve factoring; interference does the work.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 39 and 40}
Quantum phase estimation (QPE) with $t = 3$ counting qubits is applied to a unitary $U$ and an eigenvector $\ket u$ with
$U\ket u = e^{2\pi i\varphi}\ket u$, $0 \le \varphi < 1$. After the Hadamards, the controlled-$U^{2^j}$ gates and the inverse QFT, the counting register is
measured and gives $y \in \{0, \dots, 7\}$ with probability
\[ P(y) = \Big|\frac18\sum_{x=0}^{7}e^{2\pi ix(\varphi - y/8)}\Big|^2 = \frac{\sin^2\big(8\pi(\varphi - y/8)\big)}{64\,\sin^2\big(\pi(\varphi - y/8)\big)}\quad(P = 1\text{ if }\varphi = y/8). \]
The estimate of the phase is $y/8$; $y$ is written in binary with the most significant bit first.
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{39}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{QPE: exact phase}
For $\varphi = 3/8$ the measurement gives
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$y = 3$ (bits $011$) with probability $1$ & \optlabel{B}\,$y = 6$ (bits $110$) with probability $1$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$y = 3$ with probability $1/2$ & \optlabel{D}\,$y = 3$ or $y = 4$ with probability $1/2$ each
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $y = 3$ (bits $011$) with probability $1$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} QPE is exact when the phase has a $t$-bit binary expansion.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\varphi = 3/8 = 0.011_2$; $P(y) = 1$ for $y = 8\varphi = 3$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\varphi = 3/8 = 0.011_2$ is exactly representable with three bits, so all terms in the sum have phase $0$ for $y = 3$: $P(3) = 1$, and $P(y) = 0$ for every
other $y$ (the geometric sum of eighth roots of unity vanishes). $110$ is the bit-reversed string --- the inverse QFT's final SWAPs make the most significant
bit come first.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $110$ is the bit-reversed string; the notebook's inverse QFT includes the SWAPs, so $y = 3$ is read MSB first.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] For an exactly representable phase all amplitude interferes constructively at $y = 3$; probability $1$, not $1/2$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Splitting between $3$ and $4$ happens for $\varphi$ halfway between grid points ($7/16$), not for $3/8$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} If $r$ divides $2^t$, Shor's outcomes are exactly $s2^t/r$ (as for $N = 15$).
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{40}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{QPE: inexact phase}
For $\varphi = 1/3$ the most likely outcome and its probability are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$y = 3$ with $P \approx 0.69$ & \optlabel{B}\,$y = 3$ with $P \approx 0.41$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$y = 2$ or $3$ with $P = 1/2$ each & \optlabel{D}\,$y = 3$ with $P = 1$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $y = 3$ with $P \approx 0.69$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} For phases that are not multiples of $2^{-t}$ the outcome distribution is a peak around $2^t\varphi$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\delta = 1/3 - 3/8 = -1/24$; $P(3) = \sin^2(\pi/3)/(64\sin^2(\pi/24)) \approx 0.688$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $8\varphi = 2.67$, nearest integer $y = 3$, $\delta = \varphi - 3/8 = -\frac{1}{24}$. $P(3) = \frac{\sin^2(8\pi/24)}{64\sin^2(\pi/24)} = \frac{\sin^2(\pi/3)}{64\sin^2(7.5^\circ)}
= \frac{0.75}{64\times0.017037} = \frac{0.75}{1.0904} \approx 0.688$. Because $1/3$ has no finite binary expansion, the probability spreads over neighbouring $y$;
$\frac{4}{\pi^2} \approx 0.41$ is only the worst-case lower bound for the nearest outcome.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $4/\pi^2 \approx 0.405$ is only the worst-case lower bound for the nearest outcome, attained when $\varphi$ lies halfway.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $P(2) \approx 0.17$ and $P(3) \approx 0.69$: $8\varphi = 2.67$ is closer to $3$ than to $2$, so the two are far from equal.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Probability $1$ needs an exactly representable phase; $1/3$ has the infinite binary expansion $0.0101\ldots_2$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Peaks have finite width; continued fractions turn the nearest $y$ into $s/r$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\newpage
