\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{61}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Beauregard qubit count}
Beauregard's circuit for Shor's algorithm uses $2n + 3$ logical qubits. For RSA-2048 ($n = 2048$) this is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$6147$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$4099$ & \optlabel{C}\,$4096$ & \optlabel{D}\,$2051$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $4099$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Logical-qubit counts of Shor circuits are linear in the bit length $n$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Beauregard: $2n + 3$; $n = 2048$: $4099$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $2\times2048 + 3 = 4099$. $6147 = 3\times2048 + 3$ resembles the $3n$ register count of \texttt{Shor.ipynb} ($6144$). These are \emph{logical}
(error-corrected) qubits; the physical count is orders of magnitude larger.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $6147 = 3n + 3$; the $3n$ register count belongs to the notebook's construction, not Beauregard's.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $4096 = 2n$ forgets the three extra qubits (carry/ancilla and the recycled control).
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $2051 = n + 3$ omits one of the two $n$-qubit registers (work register and adder register).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Thousands of logical qubits --- each made of hundreds to thousands of physical qubits.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{62}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Published RSA-2048 estimates}
Which pair of published resource estimates for factoring RSA-2048 is correct?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Gidney (2025): about $20$ billion qubits in about $8$ hours
\item[\optlabel{B}] both estimates state that RSA-2048 was factored on existing hardware
\item[\correctlabel{C}] Gidney and Ekerå (2019): about $20$ million noisy qubits in about $8$ hours; Gidney (2025): fewer than one million noisy qubits in less than a week
\item[\optlabel{D}] Gidney and Ekerå (2019): $4099$ physical qubits in one second
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} Gidney and Ekerå (2019): about $20$ million noisy qubits in about $8$ hours; Gidney (2025): fewer than one million noisy qubits in less than a week

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Published resource estimates are model-based projections, not experimental results.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} GE2019: $\approx2\times10^7$ physical qubits, $\approx8$ h; Gidney 2025: $<10^6$ physical qubits, $<1$ week.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Both are \emph{estimates} under explicit assumptions (surface code, physical error rate $10^{-3}$, $\mu$s cycle times), not experiments. Gidney--Ekerå 2019:
$\approx 20$ million physical qubits, $\approx 8$ hours. Gidney 2025 (approximate residue arithmetic, yoked surface codes, magic-state cultivation): $< 1$
million qubits, $< 1$ week. No cryptographically relevant number has been factored by Shor's algorithm.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] The 2025 estimate \emph{lowered} the qubit count to under one million; $20$ billion is fabricated.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] No resource estimate claims an actual factorisation of RSA-2048; none has been performed.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $4099$ is Beauregard's \emph{logical} count; GE2019 required about $20$ million physical qubits and hours, not seconds.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Distinguish estimates from demonstrations: RSA-2048 remains unfactored.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{63}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$O(n^3)$ scaling}
With schoolbook arithmetic, modular exponentiation costs $O(n^3)$ gates. Doubling the bit length $n$ of $N$ multiplies the gate count by about
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$2$ & \optlabel{B}\,$2^{n}$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$8$ & \optlabel{D}\,$4$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $8$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Polynomial scaling: $O(n^3)$ means doubling $n$ multiplies the cost by $2^3$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $(2n)^3/n^3 = 8$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $(2n)^3 = 8n^3$. The cost is polynomial: $t = 2n$ controlled multiplications, each $O(n^2)$ gates. Classical sub-exponential algorithms (GNFS) grow much faster,
which is the source of Shor's advantage --- but only on a fault-tolerant machine. $2^n$ is the exponential cost of trial division.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $2$ would be linear scaling, $O(n)$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $2^n$ is exponential growth, the cost of brute-force methods, not of Shor's algorithm.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $4$ would be quadratic scaling, $O(n^2)$ --- e.g.\ the QFT alone.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Shor is polynomial ($O(n^3)$ or better), GNFS sub-exponential --- the gap grows with $n$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{64}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Semiclassical QFT}
In the ``semiclassical'' (one-control-qubit) implementation of the inverse QFT used by Beauregard, the $t = 2n$ counting qubits are replaced by
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] $2n$ ancilla qubits that are never measured
\item[\optlabel{B}] $n$ qubits, because the QFT needs only half the bits
\item[\optlabel{C}] no qubits: the QFT is computed classically before the circuit
\item[\correctlabel{D}] a single qubit that is measured and reset $2n$ times; earlier measurement results classically control the phase corrections
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} a single qubit that is measured and reset $2n$ times; earlier measurement results classically control the phase corrections

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The inverse QFT followed by measurement can be performed one qubit at a time with classical feed-forward.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Bit $y_k$ measured $\to$ rotations $R_1(-\pi\sum_{j}y_j2^{-(j-k)})$ on the next qubit; $3n \to 2n + 3$ qubits.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The inverse QFT followed by measurement can be done bit by bit (Griffiths--Niu): measure, then apply classically controlled phases to the next qubit.
One control qubit is recycled, so the count drops from $3n$ to about $2n + 3$ ($n$ work, $n + 2$ ancilla for the Fourier-space adder, $1$ control). The
measurement statistics are unchanged.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Ancilla qubits that are never measured would not reduce the qubit count; the point is to recycle one qubit.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The QFT needs all $2n$ bits of precision; they are measured sequentially on one qubit, not reduced to $n$ qubits.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The QFT acts on quantum amplitudes, which cannot be computed classically in advance.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Measurement plus classical control trades qubits for mid-circuit measurements.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{65}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Approximate QFT}
For $N = 21$, $a = 2$, $t = 10$, an approximate inverse QFT keeps only controlled phases between qubits at distance $k - j \le m$. With $m = 2$ the
number of controlled phases and the (re-executed, exact) success probability are
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] $17$ phases; $0.689$ (full QFT: $45$ phases, $0.817$)
\item[\optlabel{B}] $45$ phases; $0.817$
\item[\optlabel{C}] $17$ phases; $0.817$ --- truncation never changes the result
\item[\optlabel{D}] $2$ phases; $0.689$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $17$ phases; $0.689$ (full QFT: $45$ phases, $0.817$)

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The approximate QFT drops small-angle controlled phases; it reduces the gate count at a small cost in accuracy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Pairs at distance $\le2$: $9 + 8 = 17$; full $\binom{10}{2} = 45$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Distance $1$: $9$ pairs, distance $2$: $8$ pairs, total $17$ (full QFT: $\binom{10}{2} = 45$). The re-executed simulation gave success $0.689$ for $m = 2$, $0.787$ for $m = 3$,
$0.811$ for $m = 4$ and $0.817$ for the full QFT. Very small cut-offs lose accuracy; $m \approx \log_2 n$ plus a few suffices asymptotically.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $45$ phases and $0.817$ describe the full QFT, not the truncation $m = 2$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Truncation changes the amplitudes; the re-executed simulation shows a drop from $0.817$ to $0.689$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $m = 2$ is the maximum distance, not the number of gates; each distance contributes $t - d$ pairs.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Moderate cut-offs ($m \approx 4$) lose little; aggressive ones lose a lot.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{66}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Controlled phases in the QFT}
The full inverse QFT on $t = 8$ counting qubits (notebook default for $N = 15$) contains how many controlled phase gates?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$8$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$28$ & \optlabel{C}\,$64$ & \optlabel{D}\,$56$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $28$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The QFT on $t$ qubits uses one controlled phase per qubit pair.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $t(t - 1)/2 = 28$ for $t = 8$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} One for each pair $j < k$: $\binom82 = \frac{8\cdot7}{2} = 28$ --- the recorded gate count \texttt{cr1: 28}. In general $t(t - 1)/2 = O(t^2)$, which for
large $t$ is dwarfed by the $O(n^3)$ cost of the modular exponentiation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $8$ is the number of Hadamards in the inverse QFT, not of controlled phases.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $64 = t^2$ counts ordered pairs including $j = k$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $56 = t(t - 1)$ counts each unordered pair twice.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} QFT cost is $O(t^2)$ --- small compared with modular exponentiation.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{67}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Recorded gate counts}
The recorded gate counts of \texttt{Shor.ipynb} for $N = 15$ are \texttt{x: 1, ccustom\_unitary\_constant: 2, swap: 4, h: 16, cr1: 28} (and
\texttt{mz: 8}). Why are there $16$ Hadamard gates?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] $8$ create the superposition on the counting qubits and $8$ belong to the inverse QFT
\item[\optlabel{B}] $16 = 2^4$ is the dimension of the work register
\item[\optlabel{C}] each controlled multiplication contains $8$ Hadamards
\item[\optlabel{D}] Hadamards are inserted before every measurement of the work register
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $8$ create the superposition on the counting qubits and $8$ belong to the inverse QFT

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Hadamards appear at the start (superposition) and in the inverse QFT (one per qubit).

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $8 + 8 = 16$; total $1 + 2 + 4 + 16 + 28 = 51$ gates without \texttt{mz}.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $t = 8$ Hadamards start the algorithm, and the inverse QFT applies one $H$ per qubit ($8$ more). The multipliers are single custom gates (no internal $H$),
and the work register is not measured. Total gates without \texttt{mz}: $1 + 2 + 4 + 16 + 28 = 51$, depth $20$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The coincidence $16 = 2^4$ is irrelevant; the count is $t + t$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The multipliers are single \texttt{ccustom\_unitary\_constant} gates; no Hadamards are inside them.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] The work register is not measured in the notebook; only \texttt{mz(count)} appears.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Gate counts should be traced back to the circuit's structure.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{68}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{No hardware execution}
Why does \texttt{Shor.ipynb} refuse to run on hardware targets?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] CUDA-Q has no hardware targets
\item[\optlabel{B}] the inverse QFT cannot be executed on hardware
\item[\optlabel{C}] Shor's algorithm is mathematically impossible on hardware
\item[\correctlabel{D}] its modular multipliers are exact custom unitaries (permutation matrices) registered with \texttt{cudaq.register\_operation}; hardware would need them decomposed into native gates, which the notebook does not do
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} its modular multipliers are exact custom unitaries (permutation matrices) registered with \texttt{cudaq.register\_operation}; hardware would need them decomposed into native gates, which the notebook does not do

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Custom matrix gates are a simulator convenience; hardware executes only native gate sets.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} \texttt{cudaq.register\_operation(name, matrix)}; hardware $\to$ \texttt{ValueError} in the notebook.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The notebook raises a \texttt{ValueError} for hardware and points to the resource estimates. A dense $2^n\times2^n$ matrix gate is fine for a simulator but has no
native implementation; compiling it costs $O(n^2)$--$O(n^3)$ gates per multiplier. The inverse QFT itself uses standard gates.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] CUDA-Q supports several hardware providers; the restriction is the notebook's custom gates.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The inverse QFT uses $H$, controlled phases and SWAPs, which compile to native gates.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Shor's algorithm is a well-defined circuit; small instances have run on hardware with compiled (often simplified) circuits.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Running on hardware requires a gate-level multiplier --- the hard engineering part.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{69}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{CNOTs of a controlled multiplier}
In the gate-level circuit, ``multiply by $7$ modulo $15$'' is built as three left rotations of the 4 work bits (each $3$ SWAPs) followed by $X$ on all
four bits. Its controlled version, with controlled SWAPs of $8$ CNOTs and controlled-$X$ $=$ CNOT, uses how many CNOTs?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$9$ & \optlabel{B}\,$40$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$76$ & \optlabel{D}\,$72$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $76$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Count CNOTs gate by gate: controlled SWAP $= 8$, controlled $X = 1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $9\times8 + 4 = 76$; whole circuit: $76 + 48 + 3 = 127$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $9$ controlled SWAPs $\times\,8 = 72$ CNOTs, plus $4$ CNOTs for the controlled $X$ gates: $76$. (Multiplication by $7$ is valid on $y = 1, \dots, 14$:
$7y \bmod 15 = 15 - (y\cdot2^3 \bmod 15)$.) With the controlled $\times4$ ($6$ controlled SWAPs $= 48$) and the QFT SWAP ($3$) the circuit has $127$ CNOTs.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $9$ counts controlled SWAPs, not CNOTs.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $40$ would use $4$ CNOTs per controlled SWAP; a Toffoli alone needs $6$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $72$ forgets the four controlled $X$ gates.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Even multiplying a 4-bit number by $7$ costs $76$ CNOTs when controlled.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{70}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Random baseline}
In the gate-level circuit ($t = 3$, $a = 7$, $N = 15$) the counting outcome becomes uniformly random in the fully depolarized limit. The success
probability with the notebook's post-processing is then
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] $1/8$
\item[\correctlabel{B}] $3/8$: $y = 2, 4, 6$ give $r = 4$ and the factors; $y = 0$ gives nothing; odd $y$ give $r' = 8$, and $7^4 \equiv 1$ gives only trivial factors
\item[\optlabel{C}] $3/4$, the same as without noise
\item[\optlabel{D}] $0$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $3/8$: $y = 2, 4, 6$ give $r = 4$ and the factors; $y = 0$ gives nothing; odd $y$ give $r' = 8$, and $7^4 \equiv 1$ gives only trivial factors

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} A uniformly random outcome is the zero-information baseline for any noisy run.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Successful $y \in \{2, 4, 6\}$: $3/8 = 0.375$; odd $y \to 8$, $7^4 \equiv 1 \to$ trivial gcds.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $y/8$: $2/8 = 1/4$, $6/8 = 3/4$ give $4$; $4/8 = 1/2$ gives $4$ via multiples. For odd $y$ the denominator $8$ satisfies $7^8 \equiv 1$, but $7^{4} \equiv 1$, so
$\gcd(0, 15) = 15$, $\gcd(2, 15) = 1$ --- trivial. Hence $3/8 = 0.375$: a noisy run can still ``succeed'' by luck, which is why a success rate must be compared
with this random baseline.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1/8$ counts only one of the three successful outcomes.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $3/4$ is the noiseless success probability; full depolarization destroys the peaks.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0$ ignores that random outcomes can still give $r = 4$ by chance.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Compare noisy success rates with the random baseline, never with zero.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{71}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Memory for $N = 1023$}
Using the notebook's $3n$-qubit construction, the state-vector memory (16 bytes per amplitude) for $N = 1023$ is about
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$1.1$ TB ($36$ qubits) & \optlabel{B}\,$16.4$ kB \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$268$ MB ($24$ qubits) & \correctlabel{D}\,$17.2$ GB ($30$ qubits)
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $17.2$ GB ($30$ qubits)

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Memory of the full state vector: $16\cdot2^{3n}$ bytes in the notebook's construction.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $1023$: $n = 10$, $q = 30$, $M = 16\cdot2^{30} = 17.2$ GB.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $1023$ has $10$ bits, so $3n = 30$ qubits: $16\times2^{30} = 17.18\times10^9$ bytes. This matches the notebook's reverse estimate that $80$ GB allows at most
$32$ qubits, i.e.\ $N \le 1023$. $N = 1024$ would need $11$ bits and $33$ qubits ($137$ GB).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1.1$ TB corresponds to $36$ qubits, i.e.\ a $12$-bit $N$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $16.4$ kB is $16\cdot2^{10}$: it uses $n$ qubits instead of $3n$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $268$ MB corresponds to $24$ qubits, i.e.\ an $8$-bit $N$ such as $143$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Simulation memory explodes: a few more bits of $N$ exhaust any computer.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{72}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Toy RSA}
Toy RSA: $p = 5$, $q = 11$, $e = 7$. The private exponent $d$ and the ciphertext of $m = 2$ are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$d = 23$; $c = 18$ & \optlabel{B}\,$d = 3$; $c = 18$ & \optlabel{C}\,$d = 23$; $c = 14$ & \optlabel{D}\,$d = 7$; $c = 2$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $d = 23$; $c = 18$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} RSA: $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi(N)}$, $c = m^e \bmod N$, $m = c^d \bmod N$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\varphi(55) = 40$, $7\cdot23 = 161 \equiv 1$; $2^7 = 128 \equiv 18 \pmod{55}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\varphi(55) = 4\cdot10 = 40$; $7d \equiv 1 \pmod{40}$: $7\cdot23 = 161 = 4\cdot40 + 1$, so $d = 23$. $c = 2^7 \bmod 55 = 128 - 110 = 18$; check $18^{23} \bmod 55 = 2$. Shor's
algorithm breaks RSA by factoring $N = 55$, which reveals $\varphi(N)$ and hence $d$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $7\cdot3 = 21 \not\equiv 1 \pmod{40}$, so $d \ne 3$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $c = 2^7 \bmod 55 = 18$, not $14$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $d = e$ would need $49 \equiv 1 \pmod{40}$; and encryption does change the message.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Factoring $N$ gives $\varphi(N)$ and hence $d$: that is the threat.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{73}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Post-quantum standards}
Which standard specifies NIST's lattice-based key-encapsulation mechanism intended to replace RSA/ECDH key exchange?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) & \optlabel{B}\,SP 800-90A (random bit generators) \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,FIPS 197 (AES) & \optlabel{D}\,FIPS 186 (DSA/ECDSA)
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} FIPS 203 (ML-KEM)

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} NIST's post-quantum standards: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), 2024.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} ML-KEM: module learning with errors; no known efficient quantum algorithm.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} NIST published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, from CRYSTALS-Kyber), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, from Dilithium) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, from SPHINCS+) in August 2024. AES (FIPS 197) is
symmetric and not broken by Shor; FIPS 186 contains the signature schemes Shor's algorithm does break.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] SP 800-90A specifies random bit generators, not key exchange.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] FIPS 197 is AES, a symmetric cipher; it is not a key-encapsulation mechanism.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] FIPS 186 specifies DSA/ECDSA/RSA signatures --- schemes broken by Shor's algorithm.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Replace RSA/ECC key exchange by ML-KEM (often in hybrid mode).
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{74}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Impact on RSA, ECC, AES}
Which statement about the cryptographic impact of a large fault-tolerant quantum computer is correct?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] hash functions such as SHA-256 are broken by Shor's algorithm
\item[\optlabel{B}] only RSA is affected; elliptic-curve cryptography is immune
\item[\correctlabel{C}] Shor's algorithm breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography; AES is affected only by Grover's quadratic speed-up, so AES-256 remains adequate
\item[\optlabel{D}] Shor's algorithm breaks AES-256 in polynomial time
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} Shor's algorithm breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography; AES is affected only by Grover's quadratic speed-up, so AES-256 remains adequate

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Shor solves the hidden subgroup problem in abelian groups: factoring and discrete logarithms, including on elliptic curves.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Grover: $O(\sqrt{2^k})$ for a $k$-bit key: AES-256 $\to \approx2^{128}$ work.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Shor's period finding solves factoring and discrete logarithms in any abelian group, including elliptic-curve groups (ECDH, ECDSA). Symmetric ciphers and hash
functions have no such structure; Grover search gives at most a square-root speed-up, mitigated by doubling key length.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Hash functions are affected only by generic (Grover-type) speed-ups, not by Shor.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] ECC relies on discrete logarithms, which Shor's algorithm also solves (with fewer qubits than RSA of equal security).
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Shor's algorithm needs algebraic periodicity; AES has none, and Grover gives only a square-root speed-up.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Public-key cryptography falls; symmetric cryptography needs at most larger keys.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{75}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Fault-tolerance terms}
Match each fault-tolerance term (List-I) with its meaning (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & logical qubit & \textbf{(1)} & minimum number of physical errors that can cause an undetected logical error \\
\textbf{(Q)} & physical qubit & \textbf{(2)} & a special resource state that enables non-Clifford gates such as $T$ or Toffoli in the surface code \\
\textbf{(R)} & code distance $d$ & \textbf{(3)} & an error-corrected qubit encoded in many noisy qubits \\
\textbf{(S)} & magic state & \textbf{(4)} & a noisy hardware qubit with error rates around $10^{-3}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$2 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \correctlabel{D}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Fault tolerance encodes logical qubits in many physical qubits and supplies non-Clifford gates via magic states.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Surface code: $\approx2d^2$ physical qubits per logical qubit; logical error $\sim(p/p_{\text{th}})^{(d+1)/2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Logical qubit: encoded, error-corrected (3); physical qubit: the noisy hardware element (4); code distance: the number of errors needed for an undetected
logical error --- a surface-code patch uses about $2d^2$ physical qubits (1); magic states: distilled or cultivated resources for $T$/Toffoli (2). Shor's
arithmetic is dominated by Toffoli gates, so magic-state production dominates its cost.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] This swaps code distance and magic states; the distance is a number of errors, magic states are resources.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] This gives the physical qubit the meaning of code distance; a physical qubit is the noisy hardware element.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] This swaps logical and physical qubits; the logical qubit is the encoded one.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Shor's cost on real hardware is dominated by error correction and magic states.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{76}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Qubit counts of constructions}
Match each construction for an $n$-bit $N$ (List-I) with its logical-qubit count (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & \texttt{Shor.ipynb} ($t = 2n$ counting $+$ $n$ work) & \textbf{(1)} & $n + 1$ \\
\textbf{(Q)} & Beauregard (2003) & \textbf{(2)} & $3n + 0.002\,n\log_2 n$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & Gidney--Ekerå (2019) & \textbf{(3)} & $3n$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & one recycled counting qubit $+$ $n$ work qubits with exact (oracle) multipliers & \textbf{(4)} & $2n + 3$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$2, R$\to$4, S$\to$1 \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$2, S$\to$1
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Different constructions trade qubits for gates and measurements.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $3n$ (notebook), $2n + 3$ (Beauregard), $3n + 0.002n\log_2n$ (GE2019), $n + 1$ (idealised semiclassical).

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Notebook: $2n + n = 3n$ (3). Beauregard: $2n + 3$ (4). Gidney--Ekerå: $3n + 0.002n\log_2 n$, about $6190$ for $n = 2048$ (2). With the semiclassical QFT and
idealised matrix multipliers one needs only $n + 1$ (1) --- but real multipliers need ancilla qubits.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] This swaps Gidney--Ekerå and the idealised semiclassical count.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] This swaps Beauregard and Gidney--Ekerå; GE2019 uses slightly more than $3n$ qubits but far fewer gates.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] This swaps the notebook and Beauregard: the notebook uses $t + n = 3n$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Qubit counts alone do not decide feasibility; gate counts and error rates matter too.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{77}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Harvest now, decrypt later}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} Migrating to post-quantum cryptography is urgent even though no current quantum computer can run Shor's algorithm at
cryptographic sizes.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} Shor's algorithm also solves the discrete-logarithm problem.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\correctlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Data with long confidentiality lifetimes is already at risk from future quantum computers.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Urgent if (data lifetime) $+$ (migration time) $>$ (time to a cryptographically relevant quantum computer).

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{A is true}: encrypted data recorded today can be decrypted later (``harvest now, decrypt later''), and migrations take years. \textbf{R is true}: period
finding solves discrete logarithms, so Diffie--Hellman and ECC fall too. But R does not explain the \emph{urgency} --- that comes from data lifetime and
migration time. Answer: (B).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] is wrong because R, although true, does not explain the urgency; that comes from harvest-now-decrypt-later and slow migration.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] is wrong because R is true: Shor's algorithm solves discrete logarithms.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] is wrong because A is true.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The threat is about the future decryption of today's recorded data.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{78}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Qubits and repeated squaring}
\textbf{Statement I:} In the notebook's construction, a $32$-bit $N$ needs $96$ qubits.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} Repeated squaring lets $a^x \bmod N$ be implemented with $t$ controlled multiplications by the classically precomputed constants $a^{2^j} \bmod N$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\optlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} Both Statement I and Statement II are true

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Qubit count $3n$ and the repeated-squaring structure of modular exponentiation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $3\cdot32 = 96$; $a^x = \prod_{j=0}^{t-1}(a^{2^j})^{x_j}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is true}: $3n = 96$ (the notebook's reverse estimate: $100$ qubits allow $33$ bits). \textbf{II is true}: $a^x = \prod_j(a^{2^j})^{x_j}$, so counting qubit $j$
controls the multiplication by $a^{2^j} \bmod N$, computed classically. Answer: (A).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] is wrong because both statements are true.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] is wrong because Statement II is true: the controlled multipliers by $a^{2^j}$ are exactly the notebook's construction.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] is wrong because Statement I is true: $t + n = 64 + 32 = 96$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $t$ controlled multiplications with classically precomputed constants implement $a^x \bmod N$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 79 and 80}
A gate-level version of the order-finding circuit for $N = 15$, $a = 7$ uses $t = 3$ counting qubits and $4$ work qubits. The
multiplications by $7$ and $4 = 7^2 \bmod 15$ are compiled into controlled SWAPs (each CNOT--Toffoli--CNOT, Toffoli $=$ 6 CNOTs) and CNOTs; the
inverse QFT uses $3$ CNOTs (one SWAP) and $3$ controlled phases. In total the circuit has $127$ CNOTs. It was simulated with the CUDA-Q
\texttt{density-matrix-cpu} target and a depolarizing noise model: a one-qubit channel with parameter $p$ after every $H$, $R_z$ and $X$, and a
two-qubit channel with parameter $p$ after every CNOT and controlled phase. The probability that one shot yields the factors $3 \times 5$ was
(re-executed, exact from the density matrix):
\begin{center}\begin{tabular}{lccccc}\toprule
$p$ & $0$ & $0.001$ & $0.003$ & $0.01$ & $0.03$\\\midrule
success probability & $0.750$ & $0.740$ & $0.726$ & $0.703$ & $0.665$\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{center}
If the counting register were completely random (uniform $y$), the success probability would be $0.375$. These are simulator results, not
measurements on a quantum processor.
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{79}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Error-free probability vs success}
At $p = 0.01$, the probability that \emph{all} $127$ CNOTs are free of error is about $0.99^{127}$. Compare it with the success probability.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] $0.99^{127} \approx 0.88$, equal to the success probability
\item[\correctlabel{B}] $0.99^{127} \approx 0.28$, yet the success probability is $0.703$: many errors do not change $y$ or still lead to a correct order
\item[\optlabel{C}] $0.99^{127} \approx 0.01$, so the result is pure noise
\item[\optlabel{D}] $0.99^{127} \approx 0.28$, so the success probability must be at most $0.28$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.99^{127} \approx 0.28$, yet the success probability is $0.703$: many errors do not change $y$ or still lead to a correct order

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The error-free probability bounds nothing: many errors are harmless for the final answer.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $0.99^{127} = e^{-1.276} = 0.279$; measured (simulated) success $0.703$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $0.99^{127} = e^{127\ln0.99} = e^{-1.276} = 0.279$. The success probability is not bounded by the error-free probability: errors on work qubits after their last
use, phase errors that commute with measurement, or errors that shift $y$ to another successful value do not cause failure. Also, a random $y$ still succeeds
with probability $0.375$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.99^{127} \approx 0.28$, not $0.88$; $0.88 \approx 0.99^{13}$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.99^{127} \approx 0.28$, not $0.01$; and $0.703$ is well above the random baseline $0.375$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Errors that do not change $y$, or move it to another successful value, do not cause failure; $0.703 > 0.28$ contradicts this option.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Estimate error impact by simulation, not by the naive product of gate fidelities.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{80}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Interpreting noisy results}
Which conclusion is supported by the table?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] the results show that a quantum processor factored $15$
\item[\optlabel{B}] noise increases the success probability
\item[\optlabel{C}] at $p = 0.03$ the circuit is completely random
\item[\correctlabel{D}] the success probability decreases monotonically from $0.750$ towards the random baseline $0.375$; at $p = 0.03$ it is $0.665$, still above the baseline
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} the success probability decreases monotonically from $0.750$ towards the random baseline $0.375$; at $p = 0.03$ it is $0.665$, still above the baseline

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Noise interpolates between the ideal distribution and the uniform baseline.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Ideal $0.750$; baseline $0.375$; $p = 0.03$: $0.665$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The values fall $0.750 \to 0.740 \to 0.726 \to 0.703 \to 0.665$; the gap to the uniform baseline ($0.375$) shrinks but has not vanished. These are
density-matrix \emph{simulations} with an idealised noise model --- no quantum processor was used, and factoring $15$ with a compiled circuit that uses the known
order is a demonstration, not evidence of quantum advantage.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] These are simulations on \texttt{density-matrix-cpu}; no quantum processor was used.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The values decrease with $p$; noise never helped here.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.665$ is far above the random baseline $0.375$; the circuit is not yet completely random.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Label simulated results as simulations; compare them with the right baseline.
\end{solbox}
\qsep
